lesson.title: Microphones: Converting Sound Pressure Into an Audio Signal
lesson.summary: A microphone is a transducer that converts the pressure variations of a sound wave into a matching electrical audio signal, using one of a few different physical mechanisms depending on the microphone type.
lesson.body:
A signal is any voltage or current that varies over time to carry information, and an audio signal is a signal whose variation lies within the audio frequency range and represents sound. A microphone is the device that creates that audio signal in the first place: it is a transducer, something that converts energy from one form, in this case acoustic pressure waves in the air, into another, an electrical voltage. Every microphone shares the same basic structure: a thin diaphragm that physically moves in response to the pressure variations of an incoming sound wave, coupled to some mechanism that turns that motion into a changing voltage or current.

Two mechanisms are especially common. A dynamic microphone attaches its diaphragm to a small coil of wire suspended in a magnetic field. As the diaphragm moves, the coil moves with it, and by Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction, a moving conductor in a magnetic field generates a voltage proportional to its velocity, so the coil's motion directly produces the audio signal, with no external power required. A condenser, or capacitor, microphone instead uses the diaphragm as one plate of a small parallel plate capacitor, with a fixed backplate as the other plate.

The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor is C equal to the permittivity of free space times the plate area, divided by the plate separation. Take a small condenser mic capsule with a plate area of 1 square centimeter, 0.0001 square meters, and a diaphragm to backplate spacing of 20 micrometers, 0.00002 meters, at rest. Using the permittivity of free space, 8.85 times 10 to the minus 12 farads per meter, the resting capacitance is C = (8.85e-12 times 0.0001) divided by 0.00002 = 44.25 picofarads. If an incoming sound wave pushes the diaphragm 1 micrometer closer to the backplate, the spacing shrinks to 19 micrometers, and the capacitance becomes C = (8.85e-12 times 0.0001) divided by 0.000019 = 46.58 picofarads, a change of about 2.3 picofarads, roughly a 5 percent increase. A bias circuit connected to the capsule converts that tiny, continuously changing capacitance into a correspondingly changing voltage, which is the microphone's audio signal output.

The choice between dynamic and condenser, and other types such as piezoelectric microphones, which generate a voltage directly from mechanical stress on a crystal, affects sensitivity, whether external power is needed, frequency response, and durability, but every one of them is doing the same fundamental job described here: turning the motion of a diaphragm driven by sound pressure into an audio signal.
